subtitle: "Part III Blind Diagnostic Assessment (Chapters 09–13 · Untagged Contest Problems, 燃やす埋める Compilation & Failure-Mode Triage)"
---

When you solve an exercise at the end of [Chapter 9](../chapters/ch09-maximum-weight-closure-project-selection.qmd) ("Maximum-Weight Closure and Project Selection") or [Chapter 11](../chapters/ch11-bipartite-variable-inversion-supermodular-rescue.qmd) ("Bipartite Variable Inversion and Supermodular Rescue"), the chapter title itself tells you which algebraic transformation to apply. Before reading the problem statement, you already know whether to orient implication arcs $u \xrightarrow{\infty} v$, introduce a subset-bonus hub node, flip the indicator variables $y_j = 1 - x_j$ on one side of a bipartite graph (`二部グラフの片側反転`), or expand discrete heights into unary threshold chains $z_{i,t} = [h_i \ge t]$ (`切糕`).

In a live ICPC, NOI, Codeforces, or AtCoder contest, **problems arrive completely untagged**. Worse, Part III problems rarely mention graphs, flows, or cuts at all: they are phrased as discrete optimization over binary choices $x_i \in \{0, 1\}$, ternary sign assignments $s_i \in \{-1, 0, +1\}$, or integer height fields $h_i \in \{1, \dots, K\}$. Your decisive competitive skill is **blind algebraic-to-cut compilation** (`燃やす埋める` / Pseudo-Boolean Min-Cut Compilation): translating English profit/penalty clauses into a pseudo-Boolean polynomial, testing submodularity ($B + C \ge A + D$) or convexity ($\Delta^2 \phi \ge 0$), and compiling that polynomial into an exact directed $s$-$t$ cut network without falling into any of the Part III failure modes (`FM-09`–`FM-13`)—while also recognizing **non-flow decoys** where greedy exchange or 2D prefix/monotone-stack enumeration outperforms network flow.

::: {.callout-important title="How to Use This Blind Recognition Checkpoint"}
1. **Zero Visible Chapter or Technique Spoilers**: None of the eight problem headers or statements in Section 2 reveal which chapter (`Ch 09`–`Ch 13`) applies, or whether the problem is a **non-flow diagnostic decoy**.
2. **Execute the 3-Pass Blind Protocol Before Peeking**: For each problem (`#209`–`#216`), spend 5–10 minutes on scratch paper completing three passes before opening any dropdown:
   - *Pass 1 (Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Triage)*: What are the decision variables (binary $x_i \in \{0, 1\}$, 4-layer chain states, or $K$-level integer heights $h_i$), what are the scale bounds ($N, M, K$), and does a greedy exchange or monotone-stack sweep solve it faster than Dinic?
   - *Pass 2 (Intermediate Pseudo-Boolean / Level-Set Polynomial)*: Write the objective as $\text{BaseProfit} - \text{Penalty}(x)$ in terms of cut indicators $x_i \in \{0, 1\}$ (where $x_i = 0 \iff i \in S$ and $x_i = 1 \iff i \in T$) or unary threshold indicators $z_{i,t} = [h_i \ge t]$ ($1 = z_{i,0} \ge z_{i,1} \ge \dots \ge z_{i,K} \ge z_{i,K+1} = 0$).
   - *Pass 3 (Submodularity & Monotonicity Audit)*: Check every pairwise interaction $c_{00}(1-x_u)(1-x_v) + c_{01}(1-x_u)x_v + c_{10}x_u(1-x_v) + c_{11}x_u x_v$. Is $c_{01} + c_{10} \ge c_{00} + c_{11}$ directly (`Ch 10`), or is $c_{00} + c_{11} > c_{01} + c_{10}$ on a bipartite conflict graph requiring variable inversion $y_v = 1 - x_v$ (`Ch 11`)? On multi-state chains, have you included the reverse monotonicity locks $(i, t+1) \xrightarrow{\infty} (i, t)$ (`Ch 12`) and verified convexity $\Delta^2 \phi \ge 0$ (`Ch 13`)?
3. **3-Tier Progressive Unmasking**:
   - Open **Hint 1 (Diagnostic Signal & Chapter Reveal)** only if you cannot determine which Part III paradigm (`Ch 09`–`Ch 13` or non-flow decoy) governs the problem.
   - Open **Hint 2 (Intermediate Algebraic / Pseudo-Boolean Model)** to verify your cut polynomial and variable orientation before drawing vertices and edges.
   - Open **Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution** to check your mechanical graph compilation, hand-trace a small example ($N \le 4$), and audit your code against the broken-gadget counterexamples (`FM-09`–`FM-13`).
:::

## 1. Rapid-Fire Diagnostic Triage Drills (`FM-09`–`FM-13`)

Before tackling the eight full contest problems in Section 2, test your diagnostic reflexes on six short modelling scenarios covering the five chapters of Part III. Each scenario either contains a subtle **cut-compilation bug** (`FM-09`–`FM-13`) or asks you to discriminate between competing Part III paradigms. Formulate your diagnosis before expanding the answer callout.

---

### Drill 1.1 — The Unreachable Positive-Cycle Trap in Max-Weight Closure

In a grid defense game (`Luogu P2805 [NOI2009] 植物大战僵尸`), eating plant $u$ yields net score $w_u \in \mathbb{Z}$, and plant $u$ can only be eaten after every plant $v$ that protects $u$ (or sits to the right of $u$ in the same row) has already been eaten. A contestant wires $S \xrightarrow{w_u} u$ for $w_u > 0$, $u \xrightarrow{-w_u} T$ for $w_u < 0$, and $u \xrightarrow{\infty} v$ whenever eating $u$ requires eating $v$. They run Dinic directly and output $\sum_{w_u > 0} w_u - \text{MinCut}(S, T)$, getting `Wrong Answer` on every test case containing a mutually protecting pair $u \leftrightarrows v$.

Why does the raw Picard closure graph fail here, and what exact pre-processing pass is required before building the flow network?

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.1"}
- **Failure Mode**: **`FM-09` (Unpruned Cycles & Downstream Descendants in Project Selection, [Chapter 9](../chapters/ch09-maximum-weight-closure-project-selection.qmd))**.
- **Mathematical Root Cause**: In the physical game, zombies eat plants **one by one in a valid topological order**. If plant $u$ protects $v$ and $v$ protects $u$ ($u \leftrightarrows v$), neither plant can ever be eaten first! Furthermore, any third plant $w$ that depends on $u$ ($w \to u \leftrightarrows v$) is also permanently locked.
  - However, in Picard's simultaneous set-closure formulation (`Ch 09.1`), the closed set $C = \{u, v, w\}$ satisfies $(x \in C \land x \to y) \implies y \in C$ trivially! If $w_u + w_v + w_w > 0$, the $s$-$t$ min-cut happily leaves $\{u, v, w\}$ on the $S$-side and collects their positive weight even though no valid sequential eating order exists.
- **Mandatory Defensive Fix (`Ch 09.3`)**: Before constructing the flow network, run **Kahn's topological sort (indegree queue)** on the prerequisite graph (where edges point from *prerequisite* $v \to \text{dependent } u$). Any vertex $u$ that is **not** visited by Kahn's algorithm belongs either to a directed cycle or to the downstream shadow of a directed cycle; all such vertices must be **deleted** before wiring $S$ and $T$.
::::

---

### Drill 1.2 — The Reversed $\infty$-Arc Disaster on $T$-Side Subset Bonuses

In a binary partitioning problem (`Codeforces 311 E Biologist` / `Luogu P1361 小M的作物`), choosing $x_i = 0$ ($i \in S$) or $x_i = 1$ ($i \in T$) grants individual payoffs, and a bonus clause $j$ grants an extra reward $W_j > 0$ if **every** variable in subset $A_j$ is assigned $x_u = 1$ ($u \in T$). A contestant creates an auxiliary hub vertex $B_j$, connects $B_j \xrightarrow{W_j} T$, and connects $B_j \xrightarrow{\infty} u$ for every $u \in A_j$.

What happens to the minimum cut of this network, and how must the $\infty$-arcs be oriented?

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.2"}
- **Failure Mode**: **`FM-10` (Inverted $\infty$-Arc Orientation on $T$-Side Clause Hubs, [Chapter 10](../chapters/ch10-pseudo-boolean-cuts-submodularity-burn-bury.qmd))**.
- **Why $B_j \xrightarrow{\infty} u$ Fails Completely**: In an $s$-$t$ cut $(S, T)$, an arc pays its capacity only when its **tail is in $S$ and its head is in $T$**.
  - If you wire $B_j \xrightarrow{\infty} u$ and $B_j \xrightarrow{W_j} T$, there is **zero incoming capacity into $B_j$ from $S$**!
  - Placing $B_j \in T$ produces cut cost $0$ on $B_j \xrightarrow{\infty} u$ (since tail $B_j \in T$) and cut cost $0$ on $B_j \xrightarrow{W_j} T$ (both endpoints in $T$), regardless of whether $u \in S$ or $u \in T$! Thus the penalty $W_j$ is **never paid**, and the solver collects the bonus $W_j$ for free even when every $u \in A_j$ is in $S$.
- **Exact Rule (`Ch 10.3`)**:
  - **All-$S$ ($x_u = 0$) Bonus Hub $B_A$**: Flow must go $S \xrightarrow{W_j} B_A \xrightarrow{\infty} u$ ($\forall u \in A_j$). If any $u \in T$, placing $B_A \in S$ crosses $B_A \xrightarrow{\infty} u$ (cost $\infty$), forcing $B_A \in T$ and cutting $S \xrightarrow{W_j} B_A$ at cost $W_j$.
  - **All-$T$ ($x_u = 1$) Bonus Hub $B_B$**: Flow must go $u \xrightarrow{\infty} B_B \xrightarrow{W_j} T$ ($\forall u \in A_j$). If any $u \in S$, placing $B_B \in T$ crosses $u \xrightarrow{\infty} B_B$ (cost $\infty$), forcing $B_B \in S$ and cutting $B_B \xrightarrow{W_j} T$ at cost $W_j$.
::::

### Drill 1.3 — Submodular vs. Supermodular $2 \times 2$ Tables & The Odd-Cycle Barrier

Consider two binary decision problems over an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ with variables $x_u \in \{0, 1\}$:

- **Scenario A**: For each edge $\{u, v\} \in E$, you pay a penalty $w_{uv} > 0$ whenever $x_u = x_v$ (both $0$ or both $1$).
- **Scenario B**: You are given a triangle $V = \{1, 2, 3\}$ with edges $\{1, 2\}, \{2, 3\}, \{3, 1\}$, and for each edge you pay $w_{uv} > 0$ whenever $x_u = x_v = 1$.

Check the submodularity condition $c_{01} + c_{10} \ge c_{00} + c_{11}$ for both scenarios. Under what structural condition on $G$ can Scenario A be compiled into an $s$-$t$ min-cut, and why does Scenario B fail Bipartite Variable Inversion?

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.3"}
- **Failure Mode**: **`FM-11` (Supermodular Sign Violation & Odd-Cycle Bipartite Inversion Failure, [Chapter 11](../chapters/ch11-bipartite-variable-inversion-supermodular-rescue.qmd))**.
- **Submodularity Check**:
  - In **Scenario A**, $c_{00} = c_{11} = w_{uv} > 0$ and $c_{01} = c_{10} = 0$, so $c_{01} + c_{10} = 0 < 2w_{uv} = c_{00} + c_{11}$. In **Scenario B**, $c_{11} = w_{uv} > 0$ and $c_{00} = c_{01} = c_{10} = 0$, so $0 < w_{uv}$. Both cost tables are strictly **supermodular** (cannot be compiled directly via `Ch 10`).
- **When Bipartite Variable Inversion (`二部グラフの片側反転`, `Ch 11.1`) Rescues Scenario A**:
  - If and only if $G = (L \sqcup R, E)$ is **bipartite**, we can substitute $y_v = 1 - x_v$ for all $v \in R$ (while keeping $y_u = x_u$ for $u \in L$).
  - Then for every edge $(u, v) \in L \times R$, the condition $x_u = x_v$ transforms into $y_u \neq y_v$, flipping the supermodular penalty $w_{uv}[x_u = x_v]$ into the canonical **submodular cut penalty** $w_{uv}[y_u \neq y_v] = w_{uv} y_u(1 - y_v) + w_{uv}(1 - y_u)y_v$!
- **Why Scenario B Fails**: A triangle $\{1, 2, 3\}$ is an **odd cycle** ($C_3$). No 2-coloring of $\{1, 2, 3\}$ exists: flipping any subset of variables leaves at least one edge with both endpoints unflipped (or both flipped), keeping its penalty supermodular (indeed, minimizing $\sum_{\{u,v\} \in E} w_{uv}[x_u = x_v]$ on general graphs with odd cycles is equivalent to `MAX-CUT`, which is NP-hard).
::::

---

### Drill 1.4 — The Double-Cut Catastrophe on Multi-State Unary Chains

In a multi-state grid smoothing problem (`Luogu P3227 [HNOI2013] 切糕`), each column $u$ must be assigned a height $h_u \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ at cost $w(u, h_u) > 0$, subject to $|h_u - h_v| \le 1$ for adjacent columns $(u, v)$. A contestant builds a 3-edge chain $S = (u, 1) \xrightarrow{w(u,1)} (u, 2) \xrightarrow{w(u,2)} (u, 3) \xrightarrow{w(u,3)} (u, 4) = T$ for each column $u$, adds the diagonal smoothness arcs $(u, k) \xrightarrow{\infty} (v, k-1)$, and omits the reverse arcs $(u, k+1) \xrightarrow{\infty} (u, k)$ because "Dinic only pushes flow forward from $S$ to $T$ anyway."

Construct a 2-column numerical trace showing that omitting $(u, k+1) \xrightarrow{\infty} (u, k)$ causes the min-cut to cut a single column twice and return an impossible cost.

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.4"}
- **Failure Mode**: **`FM-12` (Omitting Reverse $\infty$-Monotonicity Arcs on Unary Chains, [Chapter 12](../chapters/ch12-multi-state-unary-chains-threshold-cuts.qmd))**.
- **2-Column Numerical Counterexample**: Let $u$ and $v$ be adjacent with $D = 1$ ($|h_u - h_v| \le 1$) and costs:
  $$w(u, \cdot) = (1, 100, 1), \qquad w(v, \cdot) = (100, 1, 100).$$
  - **True Optimal Assignment**: Since $h_v = 2$ costs $1$ and $|h_u - h_v| \le 1$, we can pick either $h_u = 1$ or $h_u = 3$ (cost $1$), giving true minimum cost $1 + 1 = 2$. Wait—what if the cross-constraint instead forces both $(u, 3) \xrightarrow{\infty} (v, 2)$ and $(v, 3) \xrightarrow{\infty} (u, 2)$, or suppose $w(u, \cdot) = (1, 100, 1)$ has $(v, 2) \in S$ and $(v, 3) \in T$ via diagonal edges $(v, 2) \xrightarrow{\infty} (u, 3)$ and $(u, 2) \xrightarrow{\infty} (v, 3)$?
  - Specifically, suppose external constraints force $(u, 2) \in T$ (so edge $(u, 1) \to (u, 2)$ is cut, cost $1$) AND force $(u, 3) \in S$ (via a diagonal $\infty$-arc from some neighbor $v$'s node in $S$ into $(u, 3)$)!
  - **Without the reverse lock $(u, 3) \xrightarrow{\infty} (u, 2)$**: The partition places $(u, 1) \in S$, $(u, 2) \in T$, $(u, 3) \in S$, $(u, 4) \in T$. The cut severs **two** edges on column $u$'s chain—$(u, 1) \to (u, 2)$ (cost $1$) and $(u, 3) \to (u, 4)$ (cost $1$)—paying $1 + 1 = 2$ to bypass the expensive middle edge $w(u, 2) = 100$, which corresponds to the **non-monotonic garbage state** $z_{u,1} = 1, z_{u,2} = 0, z_{u,3} = 1$!
- **Why Reverse $\infty$-Arcs Are Mandatory (`Ch 12.1`)**: When $(u, 2) \in T$ and $(u, 3) \in S$, the reverse arc $(u, 3) \xrightarrow{\infty} (u, 2)$ has its tail in $S$ and its head in $T$, incurring cut penalty $\infty$! Thus $(u, k+1) \xrightarrow{\infty} (u, k)$ enforces the unary threshold invariant $z_{u,1} \ge z_{u,2} \ge \dots \ge z_{u,K}$ so every column chain is cut in the forward direction **at most once** (and **exactly once** when $w(u, k) \ge 0$).
::::

### Drill 1.5 — The Non-Convex Ishikawa Penalty Trap

In a discrete signal restoration problem (`Ch 13`), each vertex $u \in V$ chooses a level $h_u \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$, and each edge $(u, v) \in E$ incurs a smooth interaction penalty $\phi(h_u - h_v)$. A programmer applies Ishikawa's cross-difference formula (`Ch 13.1`), setting the capacity of the cross-arc $(u, i) \to (v, j)$ to:
$$w_{(u, i) \to (v, j)} = \frac{1}{2}\bigl(\phi(i - j + 1) - 2\phi(i - j) + \phi(i - j - 1)\bigr)$$
for two different penalty functions:

1. **Truncated Linear Penalty**: $\phi_{\text{trunc}}(d) = \min(|d|, 2)$.
2. **Thresholded Quadratic Jump**: $\phi_{\text{conv}}(d) = |d| + 3 \cdot \max(0, |d| - 1)$.

Which of these two penalty functions produces a valid Dinic network, and what goes wrong with the other?

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.5"}
- **Failure Mode**: **`FM-13` (Non-Convex Penalty Function yielding Negative Ishikawa Capacities, [Chapter 13](../chapters/ch13-ishikawa-convex-penalties-coarea-parametric-cuts.qmd))**.
- **Second Finite Difference Audit ($\Delta^2 \phi(d) = \phi(d+1) - 2\phi(d) + \phi(d-1) \ge 0$)**:
  1. For $\phi_{\text{trunc}}(d) = \min(|d|, 2)$, the values for $d = 0, 1, 2, 3$ are $0, 1, 2, 2$. At $d = 2$:
     $$\Delta^2 \phi_{\text{trunc}}(2) = \phi_{\text{trunc}}(3) - 2\phi_{\text{trunc}}(2) + \phi_{\text{trunc}}(1) = 2 - 2(2) + 1 = -1 < 0!$$
     Because $\phi_{\text{trunc}}$ is **concave** at $|d| = 2$, the cross-arc $(u, 3) \to (v, 1)$ receives a **negative capacity** $-1/2$, which is illegal in $s$-$t$ min-cut (indeed, multi-label energy minimization with truncated penalties is NP-hard and only solvable approximately via $\alpha$-expansion).
  2. For $\phi_{\text{conv}}(d) = |d| + 3\max(0, |d|-1)$, the values for $d = 0, 1, 2, 3$ are $0, 1, 5, 9$, with first differences $+1, +4, +4$ (non-decreasing!). Thus $\Delta^2 \phi_{\text{conv}}(d) \ge 0$ for all $d \in \mathbb{Z}$, all Ishikawa cross-capacities are non-negative, and the $s$-$t$ min-cut is exact.
::::

### Drill 1.6 — Coarea Level-Set Slicing vs. Explicit Unary Chain Blowup

You are asked to choose integer values $h_1, \dots, h_N \in [0, 10^9]$ on an undirected weighted graph $G = (V, E)$ ($N \le 500, M \le 2000$) to minimize:
$$\sum_{u=1}^N c_u |h_u - b_u| + \sum_{\{u, v\} \in E} w_{uv} |h_u - h_v|,$$
where $b_u \in [0, 10^9]$ are given target values and $c_u, w_{uv} > 0$. Why does building an explicit `Ch 12` / `Ch 13` unary chain fail immediately, and how does the Discrete Coarea Theorem (`Ch 13.2`) solve this in polynomial time?

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.6"}
- **Diagnostic Contrast**: **`Ch 12` Explicit Chain ($O(N \cdot H)$ vertices) vs. `Ch 13.2` Coarea Level-Set Decoupling**.
- **Why Explicit Unary Chains Fail**: Because the coordinate range is $H = 10^9$, creating a node $(u, t)$ for every $t \in \{1, \dots, H\}$ requires $500 \times 10^9$ vertices (`Memory/Time Limit Exceeded`).
- **Coarea Level-Set Decoupling (`Ch 13.2`)**:
  - Substitute the level-set indicator $z_u(t) = [h_u > t] \in \{0, 1\}$. Since $|x - y| = \int_0^{10^9} |[x > t] - [y > t]|\,dt$, the objective decouples completely across thresholds $t$ **with zero cross-threshold edges**:
    $$\int_0^{10^9} \left( \sum_{u=1}^N c_u \bigl|z_u(t) - [b_u > t]\bigr| + \sum_{\{u,v\} \in E} w_{uv} |z_u(t) - z_v(t)| \right) dt.$$
  - Because the integrand at threshold $t$ depends **only** on the relative order of $t$ against the sorted target values $b_{(1)} < b_{(2)} < \dots < b_{(K)}$ ($K \le N \le 500$), the optimal binary cut $z(t) \in \{0, 1\}^N$ is **constant on each elementary interval** $(b_{(k)}, b_{(k+1)})$!
  - Moreover, by submodular cut nesting ($S^*(t_1) \supseteq S^*(t_2)$ for $t_1 < t_2$), all optimal $h_u^*$ belong to $\{b_1, \dots, b_N\}$ and can be found in $O(K)$ cuts (or $O(M\sqrt{N} \log N)$ via divide-and-conquer `整体二分` in `Ch 24`).
::::

Remember: **complete Pass 1 (Diagnostic Signal), Pass 2 (Algebraic Model), and Pass 3 (Submodularity/Monotonicity Check) on scratch paper before opening Hint 1.**

### Problem `#209` (`CP-III.1`) — HDU 3996: Gold Mine (`[EN]`/`[ZH]`)

- **Judge URL**: [https://acm.hdu.edu.cn/showproblem.php?pid=3996](https://acm.hdu.edu.cn/showproblem.php?pid=3996)
- **Constraints**: $T \le 15$ test cases; $L \le 25$ underground layers, $N_l \le 100$ gold deposit blocks in layer $l$ ($\sum_{l=1}^L N_l \le 2500$ blocks total). Each block $(l, i)$ has excavation cost $a_{l,i} \in [0, 10^9]$, gold value $b_{l,i} \in [0, 10^9]$, and $K_{l,i}$ dependent blocks $(l', j)$ that **cannot be mined unless $(l, i)$ is mined first** ($\sum K_{l,i} \le 5\times 10^4$). Time Limit $2.0\text{ s}$.
- **Untagged Problem Statement**:
  An open-pit gold mine consists of $L$ horizontal layers of rock. The $l$-th layer contains $N_l$ distinct ore blocks. Excavating the $i$-th block of layer $l$ costs $a_{l,i}$ dollars and yields gold worth $b_{l,i}$ dollars. Due to structural stability, each block $(l, i)$ specifies a list of $K_{l,i}$ other blocks $(l', j)$ for which $(l, i)$ is a mandatory prerequisite: none of those $K_{l,i}$ blocks $(l', j)$ may be excavated unless block $(l, i)$ is also excavated. Choose a valid subset of ore blocks to excavate so as to maximize the total net profit $\sum_{(l,i) \in C} (b_{l,i} - a_{l,i})$ (you may excavate nothing for profit $0$).

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Chapter Reveal (#209)"}

- **Target Chapter & Archetype**: [Ch 09 — Maximum-Weight Closure and Project Selection](../chapters/ch09-maximum-weight-closure-project-selection.qmd) (`§9.1` Picard's Maximum-Weight Closure on a Multi-Layer Prerequisite DAG).
- **Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal**:
  1. Each block $u = (l, i)$ is a binary decision $x_u \in \{0, 1\}$ ($x_u = 0 \iff$ excavated / $S$-side; $x_u = 1 \iff$ left in the ground / $T$-side) with an independent net profit $w_u = b_u - a_u \in [-10^9, 10^9]$.
  2. The geological constraint is a pure **closure implication**: if $(l, i)$ is a prerequisite for $(l', j)$, then excavating $(l', j)$ forces excavating $(l, i)$.
  3. Watch out for the **input direction trap (`FM-09`)**: the input for block $(l, i)$ lists the blocks $(l', j)$ that *depend on* $(l, i)$! Thus the closure implication runs from **dependent $(l', j)$ to prerequisite $(l, i)$**, NOT from $(l, i)$ to $(l', j)$!

::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic / Pseudo-Boolean Representation (#209)"}

Let $V$ be the set of all $\sum_{l=1}^L N_l \le 2500$ ore blocks, indexed by flattening $(l, i) \mapsto u \in \{1, \dots, |V|\}$, and let $w_u = b_u - a_u$. Assign cut indicator $x_u \in \{0, 1\}$ where:
$$x_u = 0 \iff u \in S \text{ (excavated)}, \qquad x_u = 1 \iff u \in T \text{ (not excavated)}.$$

1. **Objective Decomposition**:
   $$\max_{x} \sum_{u \in V} w_u (1 - x_u) = \sum_{w_u > 0} w_u - \min_{x} \left( \sum_{w_u > 0} w_u x_u + \sum_{w_u < 0} (-w_u)(1 - x_u) \right).$$
2. **Closure Penalty**: Whenever block $u = (l, i)$ is listed as a prerequisite for block $v = (l', j)$, excavating $v$ ($x_v = 0$) requires excavating $u$ ($x_u = 0$). Thus the forbidden configuration is $(x_v = 0, x_u = 1)$, which translates to the infinite cut term:
   $$\infty \cdot (1 - x_v) x_u \implies \text{directed arc } v \xrightarrow{\infty} u.$$

::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution — HDU 3996: Gold Mine (#209)"}

#### Step 1–3: Mechanical Graph Compilation (`Ch 09.1`)

1. **Vertex Indexing**: Precompute prefix offsets $\text{offset}[l] = \sum_{k=1}^{l-1} N_k$ so that block $(l, i)$ maps bijectively to vertex $u = \text{offset}[l] + i \in \{1, \dots, V_{\text{tot}}\}$, where $V_{\text{tot}} \le 2500$. Set $S = 0$ and $T = V_{\text{tot}} + 1$.
2. **Terminal Profit/Loss Arcs**: Initialize `pos_sum = 0` (`long long`!). For each block $u$ with net weight $w_u = b_u - a_u$:
   - If $w_u > 0$: add `pos_sum += w_u` and add directed arc $S \xrightarrow{w_u} u$ (cutting this arc when $u \in T$ forfeits profit $w_u$).
   - If $w_u < 0$: add directed arc $u \xrightarrow{-w_u} T$ (cutting this arc when $u \in S$ pays net loss $-w_u$).
3. **Prerequisite Closure Arcs**: When block $u = (l, i)$'s input line lists a dependent block $v = (l', j)$ (meaning $v$ cannot be mined unless $u$ is mined first), add the directed arc:
   $$v \xrightarrow{\infty} u \quad (\text{where } \infty = 10^{18}).$$
4. **Answer Extraction**: Run Dinic in 64-bit integer arithmetic (`int64_t`) and output $\text{pos\_sum} - \text{MaxFlow}(S, T)$ in $O(M \sqrt{V_{\text{tot}}})$ time.

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexamples (`FM-09`)

- **Toy Trace**: Suppose Layer 1 has block $u_1$ ($a_1 = 5, b_1 = 2 \implies w_1 = -3$) which is a prerequisite for Layer 2's two blocks $v_1$ ($a = 1, b = 4 \implies w = +3$) and $v_2$ ($a = 2, b = 6 \implies w = +4$).
  - Here $\text{pos\_sum} = 3 + 4 = 7$. We wire $S \xrightarrow{3} v_1$, $S \xrightarrow{4} v_2$, $u_1 \xrightarrow{3} T$, and dependency arcs $v_1 \xrightarrow{\infty} u_1$, $v_2 \xrightarrow{\infty} u_1$.
  - The minimum $S$-$T$ cut severs $u_1 \xrightarrow{3} T$ (cost $3$, placing $\{v_1, v_2, u_1\} \subseteq S$) rather than severing $S \to v_1$ and $S \to v_2$ (cost $3 + 4 = 7$). Thus net profit is $7 - 3 = 4$.
- **Broken Gadget Counterexample (`FM-09` — Reversing Prerequisite Arcs $u \xrightarrow{\infty} v$)**: Because the input specifies $v_1, v_2$ on $u_1$'s line, a hasty coder often wires $u_1 \xrightarrow{\infty} v_1$ and $u_1 \xrightarrow{\infty} v_2$. In our toy trace, placing $\{v_1, v_2\} \subseteq S$ and $u_1 \in T$ then has **zero** $\infty$-edges crossing from $S$ to $T$ (since $u_1 \in T$ and $v_1, v_2 \in S$ points from $T$ to $S$!), and $u_1 \xrightarrow{3} T$ has both endpoints in $T$. The broken network reports $\text{MinCut} = 0$ and claims profit $7$ by mining $v_1, v_2$ without ever excavating $u_1$! Always translate *"mining $v$ requires mining $u$"* into $(v \in S \implies u \in S) \iff v \xrightarrow{\infty} u$.

### Problem `#210` (`CP-III.2`) — Luogu P2598 `[ZJOI2009]`: 狼和羊的故事 (Wolves and Sheep) (`[ZH]`)

- **Judge URL**: [https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P2598](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P2598)
- **Constraints**: $1 \le N, M \le 100$ grid dimensions; each cell $(r, c)$ contains $a_{r,c} \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ (`0` = empty meadow, `1` = wolf, `2` = sheep). Time Limit $1.0\text{ s}$.
- **Untagged Problem Statement**:
  You are given an $N \times M$ pasture grid where each cell is occupied by a wolf (`1`), a sheep (`2`), or empty grass (`0`). Wolves can move horizontally and vertically between 4-adjacent cells, and you may install unit-length fences along the shared border between any pair of 4-adjacent cells. Find the minimum total number of unit-length fences required so that no wolf can reach any sheep by a path of unfenced 4-adjacent moves.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Chapter Reveal (#210)"}

- **Target Chapter & Archetype**: [Ch 10 — Pseudo-Boolean Cut Compilation, Submodularity & `燃やす埋める`](../chapters/ch10-pseudo-boolean-cuts-submodularity-burn-bury.qmd) (`§10.1` Binary Partition with Hard Terminal Pinning and Symmetric Pairwise Separation Penalties).
- **Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal**:
  1. Separating wolves from sheep by grid-border fences is equivalent to partitioning the $N \times M$ cells into two disjoint territories: $S$ (**Wolf territory**, $x_{r,c} = 0$) and $T$ (**Sheep territory**, $x_{r,c} = 1$).
  2. Every border between 4-adjacent cells $u$ and $v$ where one cell is in Wolf territory and the other is in Sheep territory ($x_u \neq x_v$) requires exactly $1$ unit of fence.
  3. Empty cells (`0`) have **no intrinsic preference** for $S$ or $T$, but their territory choice $x_u \in \{0, 1\}$ acts as a Steiner intermediate variable that minimizes the perimeter of the fence!

::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic / Pseudo-Boolean Representation (#210)"}

Assign a binary indicator $x_u \in \{0, 1\}$ to every grid cell $u = (r, c) \in \{1, \dots, N\} \times \{1, \dots, M\}$, where $x_u = 0 \iff u \in S$ and $x_u = 1 \iff u \in T$:

1. **Unary Terminal Pinning**:
   - If $a_u = 1$ (Wolf): $x_u = 1$ ($u \in T$) is forbidden, giving unary penalty $\infty \cdot x_u \implies S \xrightarrow{\infty} u$.
   - If $a_u = 2$ (Sheep): $x_u = 0$ ($u \in S$) is forbidden, giving unary penalty $\infty \cdot (1 - x_u) \implies u \xrightarrow{\infty} T$.
   - If $a_u = 0$ (Empty): unary penalty is $0$ (no edge to $S$ or $T$).
2. **Pairwise Submodular Fence Cost**:
   For every unordered pair of 4-adjacent cells $\{u, v\} \in E_{\text{grid}}$, a fence of cost $1$ is built iff $x_u \neq x_v$:
   $$\text{Fence}(u, v) = 1 \cdot (1 - x_u) x_v + 1 \cdot x_u (1 - x_v).$$
   Here $c_{00} = c_{11} = 0$ and $c_{01} = c_{10} = 1$, satisfying submodularity $1 + 1 \ge 0 + 0$.

::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Luogu P2598: Wolves and Sheep (#210)"}

#### Step 1–3: Mechanical Graph Compilation (`Ch 10.1`)

1. **Vertices**: Create $N M$ cell vertices $u = (r - 1)M + c \in \{1, \dots, NM\}$, plus source $S = 0$ and sink $T = NM + 1$.
2. **Terminal Pinning**:
   - For every cell $u$ with $a_u = 1$ (Wolf), add directed arc $S \xrightarrow{\infty} u$.
   - For every cell $u$ with $a_u = 2$ (Sheep), add directed arc $u \xrightarrow{\infty} T$.
3. **Symmetric Neighbor Fence Arcs**:
   - For every pair of 4-adjacent cells $\{u, v\}$, add **both** directed unit-capacity arcs $u \xrightarrow{1} v$ and $v \xrightarrow{1} u$ (implemented in Dinic as a single undirected edge of capacity $1$ in both directions, or pruned when $a_u = 2$ or $a_v = 1$).
4. **Complexity**: Since all internal edges have unit capacity $1$ and $V \le 10^4, E \le 4\times 10^4$, Dinic finds the minimum cut in $O(E \sqrt{V}) \approx 4\times 10^6$ operations ($< 15\text{ ms}$).

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexamples (`FM-10`)

- **Toy Trace**: Consider a $1 \times 3$ strip with cells $u_1 = \text{Wolf } (1)$, $u_2 = \text{Empty } (0)$, $u_3 = \text{Sheep } (2)$.
  - Graph: $S \xrightarrow{\infty} u_1 \xleftrightarrow{1} u_2 \xleftrightarrow{1} u_3 \xrightarrow{\infty} T$.
  - Either $u_2 \in S$ (cutting $u_2 \xrightarrow{1} u_3$, fence between cell 2 and 3) or $u_2 \in T$ (cutting $u_1 \xrightarrow{1} u_2$, fence between cell 1 and 2). Both yield $\text{MinCut} = 1$.
- **Broken Gadget Counterexample (`FM-10` — Omitting Empty Cells or Connecting Only Wolf $\to$ Sheep)**:
  - **Bug A (Dropping `0` cells)**: If you only include Wolf and Sheep vertices and connect adjacent Wolf–Sheep pairs, then in the $1 \times 3$ trace $(1, 0, 2)$ above, the Wolf at $u_1$ and Sheep at $u_3$ are not directly adjacent, so the graph has $0$ edges and outputs $0$ fences while the wolf walks through $u_2$ to eat the sheep!
  - **Bug B (Directed Only by Grid Coordinate $(r, c) \to (r, c+1)$)**: If you only orient grid edges rightwards/downwards $(r, c) \xrightarrow{1} (r, c+1)$ instead of bidirectionally, then placing a Sheep at $u_1 = (1, 1)$ and a Wolf at $u_2 = (1, 2)$ forces $u_1 \in T$ and $u_2 \in S$, which crosses $(1, 2) \to (1, 1)$—an arc you forgot to add! Every neutral grid border must have capacity $1$ in **both** directions ($u \xleftrightarrow{1} v$) unless one endpoint is hard-pinned to $S$ or $T$.

::::

### Problem `#211` (`CP-III.3`) — HDU 1565 / Luogu P2774: 方格取数 (Chessboard Conflict MWIS vs. Luogu P2045 Node-Splitting Disjoint Paths Contrast) (`[ZH]`/`[EN]`)

- **Judge URL**: [https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P2774](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P2774) (`HDU 1565` / `网络流 24 题 #08`) · *Diagnostic Contrast*: [Luogu P2045 方格取数加强版](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P2045) (`POJ 3422`)
- **Constraints**: $1 \le N, M \le 100$ grid dimensions; each cell $(r, c)$ has a non-negative integer weight $w_{r,c} \in [0, 10^5]$. Time Limit $1.0\text{ s}$.
- **Untagged Problem Statement**:
  You are given an $N \times M$ grid of non-negative integers $w_{r,c}$. Select a subset of cells such that **no two selected cells share a common side** (i.e., no two selected cells are 4-adjacent), maximizing the sum of $w_{r,c}$ over all selected cells.
  *(Diagnostic Bonus Question: In Chinese contests, a second classic problem is called `方格取数加强版` (`Luogu P2045` / `POJ 3422`), where $K \le 10$ walkers travel from $(1, 1)$ to $(N, N)$ moving only right or down, and each cell's weight $w_{r,c}$ can be collected at most once even if multiple walkers visit it. Why does `P2774 / HDU 1565` compile to a Part III $s$-$t$ Min-Cut whereas `P2045` requires a Part V Min-Cost Max-Flow?)*

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Chapter Reveal (#211)"}

- **Target Chapter & Archetype**: [Ch 11 — Bipartite Variable Inversion and Supermodular Rescue](../chapters/ch11-bipartite-variable-inversion-supermodular-rescue.qmd) (`§11.1` Bipartite Variable Inversion `二部グラフの片側反転` / Checkerboard Maximum-Weight Independent Set).
- **Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal**:
  1. Let $x_u \in \{0, 1\}$ indicate whether cell $u = (r, c)$ is selected ($x_u = 1$) or discarded ($x_u = 0$). Each cell grants profit $w_u x_u$, and each 4-adjacent pair $\{u, v\}$ forbids $x_u = x_v = 1$, which is a **supermodular penalty** $\infty \cdot x_u x_v$ ($c_{11} = \infty > 0 = c_{01} + c_{10}$).
  2. Why can we rescue this supermodular penalty? Because the 4-adjacency grid graph is **bipartite** under the checkerboard parity coloring $\operatorname{col}(r, c) = (r + c) \bmod 2$!
  3. By contrasts, in `Luogu P2045 方格取数加强版`, the decision variables are $K$ conserved **monotone $(1,1) \leadsto (N,N)$ paths** (flow conservation with throughput $K$) that maximize collected weight—an optimization over *flows* (Part V MCMF with node-splitting $(u_{\text{in}} \to u_{\text{out}})$ into a $(1, -w_u)$ reward arc and an $(\infty, 0)$ bypass arc), NOT an optimization over *cuts*!

::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic / Bipartite Inversion Model (#211)"}

1. **Supermodular Original Polynomial**:
   $$\max_{x \in \{0,1\}^{NM}} \sum_{u} w_u x_u - \sum_{\{u,v\} \in E_{\text{grid}}} \infty \cdot x_u x_v = \sum_{u} w_u - \min_{x} \left( \sum_{u} w_u (1 - x_u) + \sum_{\{u,v\} \in E_{\text{grid}}} \infty \cdot x_u x_v \right).$$
2. **Bipartite Variable Inversion (`Ch 11.1`)**:
   Partition the grid into Even cells $L = \{(r, c) : (r + c) \equiv 0 \pmod 2\}$ and Odd cells $R = \{(r, c) : (r + c) \equiv 1 \pmod 2\}$. Define cut indicators $y_w \in \{0, 1\}$ ($y_w = 0 \iff w \in S$, $y_w = 1 \iff w \in T$) by **flipping $R$**:
   $$y_u = 1 - x_u \quad (\forall u \in L), \qquad y_v = x_v \quad (\forall v \in R).$$
   - Thus a cell $u \in L$ is **selected** ($x_u = 1$) iff $y_u = 0$ ($u \in S$), and forfeits $w_u$ when $y_u = 1$ ($u \in T$, cutting $S \xrightarrow{w_u} u$).
   - An Odd cell $v \in R$ is **selected** ($x_v = 1$) iff $y_v = 1$ ($v \in T$), and forfeits $w_v$ when $y_v = 0$ ($v \in S$, cutting $v \xrightarrow{w_v} T$).
   - Most importantly, for every grid edge $(u, v) \in L \times R$, the supermodular conflict $\infty \cdot x_u x_v$ becomes:
     $$\infty \cdot (1 - y_u) y_v,$$
     which is the **canonical submodular cut term** for a single directed arc $u \xrightarrow{\infty} v$!

::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution — HDU 1565 / Luogu P2774 (#211)"}

#### Step 1–3: Mechanical Graph Compilation (`Ch 11.1`)

1. **Vertices & Total Weight**: Create $NM$ vertices $u \in \{1, \dots, NM\}$, source $S = 0$, sink $T = NM + 1$, and compute $\text{tot} = \sum_{r,c} w_{r,c}$ (`int64_t`).
2. **Parity-Split Terminal & Conflict Arcs**:
   - If $(r + c) \bmod 2 == 0$ (Even cell $u \in L$):
     - Add directed arc $S \xrightarrow{w_u} u$.
     - For each of the 4 neighbors $v \in R$ of $u$, add directed arc $u \xrightarrow{\infty} v$.
   - If $(r + c) \bmod 2 == 1$ (Odd cell $v \in R$):
     - Add directed arc $v \xrightarrow{w_v} T$.
3. **Output**: Return $\text{tot} - \text{MaxFlow}(S, T)$ in $O(NM \sqrt{NM})$ time.
4. **Side-by-Side Contrast with `Luogu P2045 方格取数加强版` (`Ch 20.1` Node-Splitting MCMF)**:
   - In `Luogu P2045` ($K$ monotone paths from $(1,1)$ to $(N,N)$ collecting each cell's value once), split each cell $u$ into $u_{\text{in}} \to u_{\text{out}}$ with **two parallel arcs**: one reward arc of `(cap = 1, cost = -w_u)` and one repeat-visit bypass arc of `(cap = inf, cost = 0)`, then connect $u_{\text{out}} \to v_{\text{in}}$ `(cap = inf, cost = 0)` for right/down neighbors and send $K$ units of flow via MCMF!

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexamples (`FM-11`)

- **Toy Trace**: Consider a $1 \times 2$ board with $w_{1,1} = 10$ (Even, $u_1 \in L$) and $w_{1,2} = 7$ (Odd, $v_2 \in R$).
  - Graph: $S \xrightarrow{10} u_1 \xrightarrow{\infty} v_2 \xrightarrow{7} T$, with $\text{tot} = 17$.
  - Minimum cut severs $v_2 \xrightarrow{7} T$ (cost $7$, so $u_1, v_2 \in S$, meaning $x_{u_1} = 1 - y_{u_1} = 1$ selected and $x_{v_2} = y_{v_2} = 0$ discarded). Maximum independent weight is $17 - 7 = 10$.
- **Broken Gadget Counterexample (`FM-11` — Bidirectional $\infty$-Arcs Between Even and Odd Cells)**: Suppose a coder wires **undirected** $\infty$-edges ($u_1 \xrightarrow{\infty} v_2$ AND $v_2 \xrightarrow{\infty} u_1$) between adjacent cells. Then in the $1 \times 2$ board above, no matter whether $\{u_1, v_2\}$ are placed in $(S, T)$ or $(T, S)$, one of the two $\infty$-arcs crosses from $S$ to $T$! This forces $y_{u_1} = y_{v_2}$ (meaning one cell is selected and one is discarded? Wait: if $y_{u_1} = y_{v_2} = 0$, then $x_{u_1} = 1, x_{v_2} = 0$; if $y_{u_1} = y_{v_2} = 1$, then $x_{u_1} = 0, x_{v_2} = 1$—it **forbids discarding both cells** $x_{u_1} = x_{v_2} = 0$, which requires $y_{u_1} = 1 \in T$ and $y_{v_2} = 0 \in S$!). On a $1 \times 3$ board $(10, 1, 10)$ where both endpoints $(1,1)$ and $(1,3)$ should be selected ($x_1 = x_3 = 1 \implies y_1 = y_3 = 0 \in S$) and the middle cell $(1,2)$ discarded ($x_2 = 0 \implies y_2 = 0 \in S$), wait—if $(1,2)$ is discarded, what if an Odd cell and an Even cell both need to be discarded ($x_u = x_v = 0 \implies y_u = 1 \in T, y_v = 0 \in S$)? With the reverse arc $v \xrightarrow{\infty} u$, having $v \in S$ and $u \in T$ costs $\infty$, making it **impossible to discard two adjacent cells simultaneously**! Always orient conflict arcs strictly $L \xrightarrow{\infty} R$.

::::

### Problem `#212` (`CP-III.4`) — Luogu P3756 `[CQOI2017]`: 老C的方块 (Old C's Tetrominoes) (`[ZH]`)

- **Judge URL**: [https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P3756](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P3756)
- **Constraints**: Grid dimensions $C, R \le 10^9$ (sparse grid!), with $N \le 10^5$ present cells $(x_i, y_i)$ ($1 \le x_i \le C, 1 \le y_i \le R$), each having a positive removal cost $w_i \in [1, 10^4]$. Time Limit $1.0\text{ s}$.
- **Untagged Problem Statement**:
  Old C has a sparse $C \times R$ grid containing $N$ unit squares at coordinates $(x_i, y_i)$, where deleting the $i$-th square costs $w_i$. In this grid, the vertical border between cell $(x, y)$ and cell $(x+1, y)$ is drawn as a **bold special line** whenever:
  $$(x \bmod 4 = 1 \text{ and } y \bmod 2 = 1) \quad \text{or} \quad (x \bmod 4 = 3 \text{ and } y \bmod 2 = 0).$$
  A configuration of 4 remaining squares is called **offensive** if it forms a connected 4-square tetromino (T, L, J, S, Z, or I shape) that **straddles a bold special vertical line**—precisely, it consists of the two squares $\{u_2, u_3\}$ on the left and right of a bold vertical line, together with one additional 4-adjacent square $u_1$ attached to $u_2$ and one additional 4-adjacent square $u_4$ attached to $u_3$. Delete a subset of squares of minimum total cost so that **no offensive 4-square tetromino remains**.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Chapter Reveal (#212)"}

- **Target Chapters & Archetype**: [Ch 11 — Bipartite Variable Inversion](../chapters/ch11-bipartite-variable-inversion-supermodular-rescue.qmd) + [Ch 12 — Multi-State Unary Chains & Layered Cut Compilation](../chapters/ch12-multi-state-unary-chains-threshold-cuts.qmd) (`§12.3` 4-Layer Colored Chain Cut + `Ch 03` Vertex Splitting $u_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{w_u} u_{\text{out}}$).
- **Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal**:
  1. Look closely at the parity definition of the bold vertical lines! Every bold vertical line separates a left square $u_2 = (x, y)$ with $(x \bmod 2 = 1)$ from a right square $u_3 = (x+1, y)$ with $(x+1 \bmod 2 = 0)$ where $x \equiv 1 \pmod 4, y \equiv 1 \pmod 2$ or $x \equiv 3 \pmod 4, y \equiv 0 \pmod 2$.
  2. Notice that the two central squares $(u_2, u_3)$ of **every** bold vertical line are disjoint from the central squares of every other bold vertical line, and every neighbor $u_1$ of $u_2$ (other than $u_3$) and every neighbor $u_4$ of $u_3$ (other than $u_2$) can be assigned to **4 globally disjoint color classes** $V_1, V_2, V_3, V_4$ based on $(x \bmod 4, y \bmod 2)$!
  3. Consequently, **every offensive 4-square pattern is a directed path $u_1 \to u_2 \to u_3 \to u_4$ across a 4-layered DAG $V_1 \to V_2 \to V_3 \to V_4$**! Deleting minimum-weight vertices to destroy all $V_1 \to V_2 \to V_3 \to V_4$ paths is a pure vertex-split $s$-$t$ Min-Cut!

::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic / 4-Color Layer Classification (#212)"}

Classify every cell $(x, y)$ into one of four disjoint color classes $c(x, y) \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ based on its row parity $y \bmod 2$ and column residue $x \bmod 4$:

- On **Odd rows ($y \bmod 2 = 1$)**, bold lines lie between $x \equiv 1$ and $x \equiv 2 \pmod 4$:
  - $x \equiv 1 \pmod 4 \implies \text{Color } 2$ (left of bold line)
  - $x \equiv 2 \pmod 4 \implies \text{Color } 3$ (right of bold line)
  - $x \equiv 0 \pmod 4 \implies \text{Color } 1$ (left neighbor of Color 2)
  - $x \equiv 3 \pmod 4 \implies \text{Color } 4$ (right neighbor of Color 3)
- On **Even rows ($y \bmod 2 = 0$)**, bold lines lie between $x \equiv 3$ and $x \equiv 0 \pmod 4$:
  - $x \equiv 3 \pmod 4 \implies \text{Color } 2$ (left of bold line)
  - $x \equiv 0 \pmod 4 \implies \text{Color } 3$ (right of bold line)
  - $x \equiv 2 \pmod 4 \implies \text{Color } 1$ (left neighbor of Color 2)
  - $x \equiv 1 \pmod 4 \implies \text{Color } 4$ (right neighbor of Color 3)

Verify what happens to vertical neighbors $(x, y \pm 1)$ of Color 2 and Color 3!
- If $(x, y)$ has **Color 2** (say $y$ odd, $x \equiv 1 \pmod 4$), then its vertical neighbors $(x, y \pm 1)$ have $y \pm 1$ even and $x \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, which has **Color 1**? Wait: on even rows, $x \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ is adjacent to $x \equiv 1$ of odd rows (Color 2) and $x \equiv 2$ of odd rows (Color 3):
  - Any 4-neighbor of a **Color 2** cell (except its bold-line partner in Color 3) lies at $(x-1, y)$ or $(x, y \pm 1)$, both of which have $x \bmod 4 \in \{0 \text{ (odd } y\text{)}, 1 \text{ (even } y\text{)}\}$! So if we label **all** non-Color-3 neighbors of Color 2 as **Color 1**, and **all** non-Color-2 neighbors of Color 3 as **Color 4**:
    - Odd $y$: $x \bmod 4 = (1 \mapsto C_2,\; 2 \mapsto C_3,\; 3 \mapsto C_4,\; 0 \mapsto C_1)$.
    - Even $y$: $x \bmod 4 = (1 \mapsto C_1,\; 2 \mapsto C_4,\; 3 \mapsto C_2,\; 0 \mapsto C_3)$.
  Let's check! If $(x, y)$ is $C_2$ (odd $y, x \equiv 1$), its left neighbor is $(odd, 0) \in C_1$, and its vertical neighbors are $(even, 1) \in C_1$! If $(x, y)$ is $C_3$ (odd $y, x \equiv 2$), its right neighbor is $(odd, 3) \in C_4$, and its vertical neighbors are $(even, 2) \in C_4$! Every single offensive 4-tetromino is now a path $C_1 \to C_2 \to C_3 \to C_4$!

::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Luogu P3756: Old C's Tetrominoes (#212)"}

#### Step 1–3: Mechanical Graph Compilation (`Ch 03.1` + `Ch 12.3`)

1. **4-Coloring Table**: Using a hash map (or sorted coordinate lookup) over the $N \le 10^5$ present cells $(x_i, y_i)$, assign each cell $i$ its color $c_i \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$:
   - If $y_i \bmod 2 == 1$: map $x_i \bmod 4 \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\} \mapsto \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$.
   - If $y_i \bmod 2 == 0$: map $x_i \bmod 4 \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\} \mapsto \{3, 1, 4, 2\}$.
2. **Vertex Splitting**: Split each present cell $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ into $i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{w_i} i_{\text{out}}$ (`2N` vertices plus $S, T$).
3. **4-Layer Chain Wiring ($S \to C_1 \to C_2 \to C_3 \to C_4 \to T$)**:
   - If $c_i = 1$: add $S \xrightarrow{\infty} i_{\text{in}}$, and for every present 4-neighbor $j$ with $c_j = 2$, add $i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} j_{\text{in}}$.
   - If $c_i = 2$: for the bold-line right neighbor $j = (x_i + 1, y_i)$ (if present, note $c_j = 3$), add $i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} j_{\text{in}}$.
   - If $c_i = 3$: for every present 4-neighbor $j$ with $c_j = 4$, add $i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} j_{\text{in}}$.
   - If $c_i = 4$: add $i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} T$.
4. **Correctness & Complexity**: Every offensive 4-cell tetromino contains exactly one cell of each color $C_1, C_2, C_3, C_4$ forming a directed $S \to T$ path of $\infty$-bridges and internal $w_i$-edges; conversely, because $C_2 \to C_3$ only crosses bold vertical lines, every $S \to T$ path corresponds to a valid offensive 4-cell tetromino! Running Dinic on $2N + 2 \le 2\times 10^5$ vertices takes $O(N \sqrt{N})$ time.

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexamples

- **Toy Trace**: Let $N = 4$ on Row $y = 1$ (odd): cells at $x = 1$ ($C_2, w = 10$), $x = 2$ ($C_3, w = 10$), $x = 3$ ($C_4, w = 5$), and on Row $y = 2$ (even): cell at $x = 1$ ($C_1, w = 3$).
  - These 4 cells form an L-tetromino straddling the bold line between $(1, 1)$ and $(2, 1)$.
  - Path in network: $S \xrightarrow{\infty} (1,2)_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{3} (1,2)_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} (1,1)_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{10} (1,1)_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} (2,1)_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{10} (2,1)_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} (3,1)_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{5} (3,1)_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} T$.
  - Minimum cut severs $(1,2)_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{3} (1,2)_{\text{out}}$ at cost $3$.
- **Broken Gadget Counterexample (Swapping $C_1$ and $C_4$ on Even Rows)**: On even rows, if you naively assign $x \equiv 2 \mapsto C_1$ and $x \equiv 1 \mapsto C_4$ (matching the left-to-right order of odd rows), then cell $(1, 2)$ (above $C_2 = (1, 1)$) gets color $C_4$ instead of $C_1$, so the vertical adjacency between $(1, 1) \in C_2$ and $(1, 2)$ is missed by the $C_1 \to C_2$ layer and vertical L/T/S/Z tetrominoes survive uncut!

### Problem `#213` (`CP-III.5`) — AtCoder ARC 147 E: Examination (`[JA]`/`[EN]`)

- **Judge URL**: [https://atcoder.jp/contests/arc147/tasks/arc147_e](https://atcoder.jp/contests/arc147/tasks/arc147_e)
- **Constraints**: $1 \le N \le 3 \times 10^5$ students; student $i$ has initial score $A_i \in [1, 10^9]$ and passing threshold $B_i \in [1, 10^9]$. Time Limit $2.0\text{ s}$.
- **Untagged Problem Statement**:
  $N$ students took an exam. Student $i$ scored $A_i$ points, and needs at least $B_i$ points to graduate. You may choose a subset of students $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ and arbitrarily permute their scores $\{A_i : i \in S\}$ among the students in $S$ so that **every** student $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ ends up with a score of at least $B_i$. Maximize the number of students $N - |S|$ whose scores are **not** swapped (or output `-1` if no valid permutation exists).

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Chapter Reveal (#213)"}

- **Target Paradigm & Archetype**: **Diagnostic Boundary (`Decoy` against `Ch 08` Hall / `Ch 12` Threshold Cut — Solved via $O(N \log N)$ Greedy Exchange Heap, previewing [Ch 23](../chapters/ch23-simulated-mcmf-regret-greedy-heap-segtree.qmd))**.
- **Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal**:
  1. Look at the scale: $N = 3 \times 10^5$ and $A_i, B_i \le 10^9$. Any explicit bipartite matching or threshold cut network has $\Omega(N^2)$ edges and immediately `TLE`s.
  2. Every student $i$ with $A_i < B_i$ **must** be included in the swapped pool $S$ (they fail if left untouched).
  3. By Hall's Marriage Theorem on the linearly ordered interval graph $(u \sim v \iff A_u \ge B_v)$, a multiset of available scores $\mathcal{A}$ can satisfy a multiset of demands $\mathcal{B}$ ($|\mathcal{A}| = |\mathcal{B}|$) if and only if when both are sorted ascending, $\mathcal{A}_{(k)} \ge \mathcal{B}_{(k)}$ for all $k$.
  4. Any student $j$ with $A_j \ge B_j$ who is recruited into $S$ acts as a **score upgrader**: they consume a small available score $a \ge B_j$ and inject a larger available score $A_j$ into $\mathcal{A}$!

::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic / Greedy Exchange Representation (#213)"}

Partition the $N$ students into:

- **Mandatory Pool $S_0 = \{i : A_i < B_i\}$**: Put their scores $A_i$ into a min-heap $\mathcal{A}$ and their thresholds $B_i$ into a min-heap $\mathcal{B}$ (note $|\mathcal{A}| = |\mathcal{B}|$).
- **Candidate Donors $D_0 = \{j : A_j \ge B_j\}$**: Sort them by threshold $B_j$ ascending.

At each step while $\mathcal{A}$ is non-empty, inspect the **smallest available score** $a = \min \mathcal{A}$ and the **smallest unmet demand** $b = \min \mathcal{B}$:

1. **Unlock Feasible Donors**: Every candidate donor $j \in D_0$ with $B_j \le a$ can be satisfied by score $a$. Push their scores $A_j$ into a max-heap $\mathcal{D}$ of unlocked donors.
2. **Match or Upgrade**:
   - If $b \le a$: since $a$ is the *weakest* score in $\mathcal{A}$ and $b$ is the *easiest* demand in $\mathcal{B}$, matching $a$ to $b$ is unconditionally optimal! Pop $a$ from $\mathcal{A}$ and pop $b$ from $\mathcal{B}$.
   - If $b > a$: score $a$ is too small to satisfy *any* demand in $\mathcal{B}$! It **must** be used to satisfy some unlocked donor $j \in \mathcal{D}$ ($B_j \le a$). To maximize the upgraded supply, pop the donor with the **largest $A_j$** from $\mathcal{D}$, use $a$ to satisfy $B_j$ (pop $a$ from $\mathcal{A}$), and push $A_j$ into $\mathcal{A}$!

::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution — AtCoder ARC 147 E: Examination (#213)"}

#### Step 1–3: $O(N \log N)$ Priority-Queue Exchange Algorithm

1. **Initialization**:
   - Create min-heaps $\mathcal{A}$ (available scores in $S$) and $\mathcal{B}$ (unmet demands in $S$), and a max-heap $\mathcal{D}$ (available $A_j$ of unlocked donors).
   - For each $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$: if $A_i < B_i$, push $A_i \to \mathcal{A}$ and $B_i \to \mathcal{B}$; otherwise append $(B_i, A_i)$ to list `donors`.
   - Sort `donors` in ascending order of $B_j$, and maintain pointer `ptr = 0`. Initialize `kept_donors = |donors|`.
2. **Sweep & Exchange Loop**:
   - While $\mathcal{A}$ is not empty:
     - Let $a = \mathcal{A}.\text{top}()$ and $b = \mathcal{B}.\text{top}()$.
     - While $\text{ptr} < |\text{donors}|$ and $\text{donors}[\text{ptr}].B \le a$:
       - Push $\text{donors}[\text{ptr}].A$ into max-heap $\mathcal{D}$, and increment `ptr`.
     - If $b \le a$:
       - Pop $a$ from $\mathcal{A}$ and pop $b$ from $\mathcal{B}$ (demand $b$ is satisfied).
     - Else ($b > a$):
       - If $\mathcal{D}$ is empty, no student anywhere has threshold $\le a$; return `-1`.
       - Pop $a$ from $\mathcal{A}$ (assigned to the chosen donor's threshold $B_j \le a$).
       - Pop the maximum score $A_{\max}$ from $\mathcal{D}$, push $A_{\max}$ into $\mathcal{A}$, and decrement `kept_donors` by $1$.
3. **Output**: Return `kept_donors` in $O(N \log N)$ time and $O(N)$ memory.

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Diagnostic Failure Modes

- **Toy Trace**: Let $N = 3$ with Student 1: $(A_1, B_1) = (2, 4)$, Student 2: $(4, 3)$, Student 3: $(5, 2)$.
  - Failing: Student 1 $\implies \mathcal{A} = \{2\}, \mathcal{B} = \{4\}$. Donors sorted by $B$: Student 3 $(B_3 = 2, A_3 = 5)$, Student 2 $(B_2 = 3, A_2 = 4)$, `kept_donors = 2`.
  - Step 1: $a = 2, b = 4$. Unlock donors with $B_j \le 2 \implies$ Student 3 enters $\mathcal{D} = \{5\}$. Since $b = 4 > a = 2$, pop $a = 2$, pop $A_3 = 5$ from $\mathcal{D}$, push $5 \to \mathcal{A}$, `kept_donors = 1`.
  - Step 2: $a = 5, b = 4$. Unlock Student 2 ($B_2 = 3 \le 5$). Now $b = 4 \le a = 5$: pop $5$ from $\mathcal{A}$ and $4$ from $\mathcal{B}$. Loop terminates with answer `kept_donors = 1` (Student 2 keeps their score).
- **Why Flow / Matching Fails Here**: Building a bipartite graph between $A_i$ and $B_j$ has $N^2 = 9\times 10^{10}$ edges; even with prefix-tree sparsification (`Ch 22`), minimum-cost flow on $3\times 10^5$ vertices cannot beat the $O(N \log N)$ exchange heap induced by the 1D total order of scores!

### Problem `#214` (`CP-III.6`) — AtCoder ABC 225 G: X (Cross) (`[JA]`/`[EN]`)

- **Judge URL**: [https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc225/tasks/abc225_g](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc225/tasks/abc225_g)
- **Constraints**: $1 \le H, W \le 100$ grid dimensions, $1 \le C \le 10^9$ diagonal stroke cost, $1 \le A_{r,c} \le 10^9$ cell reward. Time Limit $2.0\text{ s}$.
- **Untagged Problem Statement**:
  You are given an $H \times W$ grid where cell $(r, c)$ carries a positive reward $A_{r,c}$. You may choose any subset of cells on which to draw an `'X'`. Each `'X'` consists of two unit diagonal segments: a top-left-to-bottom-right (`\`) segment and a top-right-to-bottom-left (`/`) segment.
  Rather than paying for each cell's segments individually, you draw continuous diagonal lines across chosen cells: paying a flat cost $C$ allows you to draw a continuous `\` line segment of any length along a northwest-southeast diagonal, and paying $C$ allows you to draw a continuous `/` line segment of any length along a northeast-southwest diagonal (equivalently, each contiguous run of chosen cells along a `\` diagonal costs $C$, and each contiguous run of chosen cells along a `/` diagonal costs $C$). Maximize (Total Reward of Chosen Cells) $-$ (Total Cost of Diagonal Runs).

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Chapter Reveal (#214)"}

- **Target Chapters & Archetype**: [Ch 09 — Maximum-Weight Closure](../chapters/ch09-maximum-weight-closure-project-selection.qmd) + [Ch 10 — Pseudo-Boolean Cut Compilation (`燃やす埋める`)](../chapters/ch10-pseudo-boolean-cuts-submodularity-burn-bury.qmd) (`§10.4` Edge-Compressed Pairwise Savings / Contiguous Run Counting via Top-Endpoint Transitions).
- **Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal**:
  1. How do you count the number of contiguous runs of $1$s along a 1D diagonal without higher-order DP? **A contiguous run of chosen cells along a `\` diagonal starts at $(r, c)$ if and only if $(r, c)$ is chosen AND its northwest predecessor $(r-1, c-1)$ is NOT chosen!**
  2. Similarly, a contiguous run of chosen cells along a `/` diagonal starts at $(r, c)$ if and only if $(r, c)$ is chosen AND its northeast predecessor $(r-1, c+1)$ is NOT chosen!
  3. Look at that algebraic term: *"$(r, c)$ is chosen ($u \in S$) and $(r-1, c-1)$ is NOT chosen ($v \in T$)"* with cost $C$ is literally a **single directed cut arc** $(r, c) \xrightarrow{C} (r-1, c-1)$!

::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic / Pseudo-Boolean Representation (#214)"}

Let $x_{r,c} \in \{0, 1\}$ be the cut indicator where $x_{r,c} = 0 \iff (r, c) \in S$ (**chosen**) and $x_{r,c} = 1 \iff (r, c) \in T$ (**not chosen**). Define boundary dummy cells outside the grid as permanently **not chosen** ($x_{0, c} = x_{r, 0} = x_{r, W+1} = 1$, i.e., pinned to $T$).

1. **Reward of Chosen Cells**:
   $$\sum_{r=1}^H \sum_{c=1}^W A_{r,c} (1 - x_{r,c}) = \sum_{r,c} A_{r,c} - \sum_{r,c} A_{r,c} x_{r,c}.$$
2. **Exact Cost of `\` and `/` Contiguous Runs**:
   Every `\` run pays $C$ at its unique topmost cell $(r, c)$ (where $x_{r,c} = 0$ and $x_{r-1, c-1} = 1$), and every `/` run pays $C$ at its unique topmost cell $(r, c)$ (where $x_{r,c} = 0$ and $x_{r-1, c+1} = 1$):
   $$\text{Cost}(x) = \sum_{r=1}^H \sum_{c=1}^W C \cdot (1 - x_{r,c}) x_{r-1, c-1} + \sum_{r=1}^H \sum_{c=1}^W C \cdot (1 - x_{r,c}) x_{r-1, c+1}.$$
   Every single penalty term in $\sum A_{r,c} x_{r,c} + \text{Cost}(x)$ is already in canonical $S \to T$ cut form!

::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution — AtCoder ABC 225 G: X (#214)"}

#### Step 1–3: Mechanical Graph Compilation (`Ch 10.4` Zero-Auxiliary-Node Form)

1. **Vertices**: Create $HW$ vertices $u(r, c) = (r - 1)W + c \in \{1, \dots, HW\}$, source $S = 0$, and sink $T = HW + 1$. Initialize $\text{tot} = \sum_{r,c} A_{r,c}$ (`int64_t`).
2. **Reward Arcs**: For each cell $(r, c)$, add directed arc $S \xrightarrow{A_{r,c}} u(r, c)$.
3. **Northwest (`\`) Run-Start Arcs**:
   - If $r > 1$ and $c > 1$: add directed arc $u(r, c) \xrightarrow{C} u(r - 1, c - 1)$.
   - Else (top row $r = 1$ or left column $c = 1$): add directed arc $u(r, c) \xrightarrow{C} T$.
4. **Northeast (`/`) Run-Start Arcs**:
   - If $r > 1$ and $c < W$: add directed arc $u(r, c) \xrightarrow{C} u(r - 1, c + 1)$.
   - Else (top row $r = 1$ or right column $c = W$): add directed arc $u(r, c) \xrightarrow{C} T$.
5. **Output**: Return $\text{tot} - \text{MaxFlow}(S, T)$ in $O(HW \sqrt{HW})$ time ($V = 10002, E \le 30000$, runs in $< 15\text{ ms}$).

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexamples

- **Toy Trace**: Let $H = 2, W = 2, C = 5$ with $A_{1,1} = 6, A_{2,2} = 7$ and $A_{1,2} = A_{2,1} = 1$.
  - Suppose we choose $(1, 1)$ and $(2, 2)$ ($\subseteq S$) and leave $(1, 2), (2, 1) \in T$.
  - Cell $(1, 1) \in S$ is on the top/left/right border? For $W = 2$, $(1, 1)$ has $r = 1$, so both its `\` and `/` arcs go to $T$: cost $C + C = 10$.
  - Cell $(2, 2) \in S$ has its `\` arc pointing to $(1, 1) \in S$ (not cut! Cost $0$, because $(2, 2)$ extends $(1, 1)$'s `\` stroke for free!) and its `/` arc pointing to $T$ (since $c = W = 2$, cut cost $C = 5$).
  - Total cut on chosen cells $= 10 + 5 = 15$; wait—since $A_{1,1} + A_{2,2} = 13 < 15$, the minimum cut actually places $(1, 1), (2, 2) \in T$ (cutting $S \to (1,1)$ and $S \to (2,2)$ for cost $13$), giving net profit $15 - 15 = 0$ (or if $C = 4$, cost is $3C = 12 < 13$, giving profit $13 - 12 = 1$).
- **Broken Gadget Counterexample (Creating $2HW$ Auxiliary Bonus Nodes with Negative Base Weights $A_{r,c} - 2C$)**: While you *can* model this as `Ch 09` Project Selection with base weight $A_{r,c} - 2C$ and $+C$ bonus nodes for $\{(r,c), (r-1,c-1)\}$ and $\{(r,c), (r-1,c+1)\}$, doing so triples the vertex count to $3HW + 2$. Worse, if you forget that a gap in a diagonal ($(1,1) \in S, (2,2) \in T, (3,3) \in S$) starts a **second** run and instead only pay $C$ once per entire diagonal via a single diagonal hub node, you falsely allow broken dashed diagonals to share a single $C$ payment!

### Problem `#215` (`CP-III.7`) — AtCoder ABC 311 G: One More Grid Task (`[JA]`/`[EN]`)

- **Judge URL**: [https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc311/tasks/abc311_g](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc311/tasks/abc311_g)
- **Constraints**: $1 \le N, M \le 300$ grid dimensions; $1 \le A_{r,c} \le 300$ positive integer weights. Time Limit $2.0\text{ s}$.
- **Untagged Problem Statement**:
  You are given an $N \times M$ grid of positive integers $A_{r,c}$. Choose an axis-aligned subrectangle $[r_1, r_2] \times [c_1, c_2]$ ($1 \le r_1 \le r_2 \le N$, $1 \le c_1 \le c_2 \le M$) to maximize the product of the **sum** of elements in the subrectangle and the **minimum** element in the subrectangle:
  $$\max_{\substack{1 \le r_1 \le r_2 \le N \\ 1 \le c_1 \le c_2 \le M}} \left( \sum_{r=r_1}^{r_2} \sum_{c=c_1}^{c_2} A_{r,c} \right) \times \left( \min_{\substack{r_1 \le r \le r_2 \\ c_1 \le c \le c_2}} A_{r,c} \right).$$

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Chapter Reveal (#215)"}

- **Target Paradigm & Archetype**: **Diagnostic Boundary (`Decoy` against `Ch 09` / `Ch 12` Threshold Closure — Solved in $O(N^2 M)$ via 2D Row-Pair Enumeration + 1D Monotone Stack / Cartesian Tree)**.
- **Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal**:
  1. Why is this **not** a minimum-cut problem? In a minimum-cut closure problem, you can select an *arbitrary closed subset* of vertices (or a union of rectangles). Here, the chosen set must be a **single contiguous axis-aligned rectangle** $[r_1, r_2] \times [c_1, c_2]$!
  2. Furthermore, all $A_{r,c} > 0$, and $N, M \le 300$ means there are only $\binom{N+1}{2} \approx 4.5 \times 10^4$ row intervals $[r_1, r_2]$!
  3. Once $[r_1, r_2]$ is fixed, each column $c \in \{1, \dots, M\}$ collapses to two numbers: its column sum $S_c = \sum_{r=r_1}^{r_2} A_{r,c} > 0$ and its column minimum $M_c = \min_{r=r_1}^{r_2} A_{r,c}$, reducing the problem to the classic $O(M)$ **Largest Histogram / Monotone Stack** sweep!

::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic / 1D Histogram Reduction (#215)"}

Fix the top row $r_1 \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ and increment the bottom row $r_2 = r_1, r_1 + 1, \dots, N$. Maintain two arrays of length $M$:
$$S_c(r_1, r_2) = \sum_{r=r_1}^{r_2} A_{r,c}, \qquad M_c(r_1, r_2) = \min_{r=r_1}^{r_2} A_{r,c}.$$

For a fixed pair $(r_1, r_2)$, we want to maximize over $1 \le c_1 \le c_2 \le M$:
$$\left( \min_{c_1 \le c \le c_2} M_c \right) \times \sum_{c=c_1}^{c_2} S_c.$$
Because $S_c > 0$ for every column $c$, if the minimum $M_{c^*}$ occurs at column $c^*$, we should expand $[c_1, c_2]$ as far left and right as possible without including any column with $M_c < M_{c^*}$! Using a **monotone increasing stack** on $M_1, \dots, M_M$ finds for every $c^*$ the first column $L_{c^*} < c^*$ with $M_{L_{c^*}} < M_{c^*}$ and the first column $R_{c^*} > c^*$ with $M_{R_{c^*}} < M_{c^*}$ in $O(M)$ total time.

::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution — AtCoder ABC 311 G (#215)"}

#### Step 1–3: $O(N^2 M)$ Row-Strip + Monotone Stack Algorithm

1. **Outer Loop over Top Row $r_1 = 1 \dots N$**:
   - Initialize $S[1..M] \gets 0$ and $M_{\text{col}}[1..M] \gets +\infty$.
2. **Inner Loop over Bottom Row $r_2 = r_1 \dots N$**:
   - For $c = 1 \dots M$: update $S[c] \mathrel{+}= A_{r_2, c}$, $M_{\text{col}}[c] \gets \min(M_{\text{col}}[c], A_{r_2, c})$, and prefix sum $P[c] = P[c-1] + S[c]$.
   - Run a single-pass **monotone increasing stack** over $c = 1 \dots M + 1$ (with sentinel $M_{\text{col}}[M+1] = 0$):
     - Whenever $M_{\text{col}}[\text{stk.top}()] \ge M_{\text{col}}[c]$, pop index $k = \text{stk.pop}()$; its right boundary is $R_k = c - 1$ and its left boundary is $L_k = (\text{stk.empty}() \text{ ? } 1 : \text{stk.top}() + 1)$.
     - Update $\text{ans} \gets \max\bigl(\text{ans},\; M_{\text{col}}[k] \times (P[R_k] - P[L_k - 1])\bigr)$.
     - Push $c$ onto `stk`.
3. **Complexity**: $O(N^2 M) = 300^3 = 2.7 \times 10^7$ primitive array operations ($< 40\text{ ms}$).

#### Step 4: Toy Trace & Why Cut Compilation Is the Wrong Tool

- **Toy Trace**: For a $1 \times 3$ row with $A = [3, 2, 4]$:
  - Prefix sums $P = [0, 3, 5, 9]$.
  - At $c = 1$: push $1$ ($M = 3$).
  - At $c = 2$ ($M = 2 < 3$): pop $k = 1$ with $[L_1, R_1] = [1, 1] \implies 3 \times 3 = 9$. Push $2$ ($M = 2$).
  - At $c = 3$ ($M = 4$): push $3$.
  - At sentinel $c = 4$ ($M = 0$): pop $k = 3$ ($[3, 3] \implies 4 \times 4 = 16$); pop $k = 2$ ($[1, 3] \implies 2 \times (3 + 2 + 4) = 18$). Max is $18$.
- **Diagnostic Lesson**: Whenever the feasible region is a **low-dimensional parametric family** (like $O(N^2 M^2)$ rectangles) rather than an exponential $2^V$ subset lattice, check whether fixing 1 or 2 coordinates reduces the remaining coordinates to a 1D greedy / monotone-stack / Kadane sweep before reaching for Dinic!

::::

### Problem `#216` (`CP-III.8`) — Codeforces 1473 F: Strange Set (`[EN]`)

- **Judge URL**: [https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1473/F](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1473/F)
- **Constraints**: $1 \le N \le 3000$ elements; $1 \le a_i \le 100$ integer values; $-10^5 \le b_i \le 10^5$ integer weights. Time Limit $2.0\text{ s}$.
- **Untagged Problem Statement**:
  You are given two arrays $a_1, \dots, a_N$ ($1 \le a_i \le 100$) and $b_1, \dots, b_N$ ($-10^5 \le b_i \le 10^5$). A subset of indices $C \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, N\}$ is called **strange** if for every index $i \in C$, every earlier index $j < i$ such that $a_j$ divides $a_i$ ($a_j \mid a_i$) also belongs to $C$. Find the maximum possible sum of weights $\sum_{i \in C} b_i$ of a strange set $C$ (the empty set $C = \emptyset$ is valid and has sum $0$).

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Chapter Reveal (#216)"}

- **Target Chapter & Archetype**: [Ch 09 — Maximum-Weight Closure and Project Selection](../chapters/ch09-maximum-weight-closure-project-selection.qmd) (`§9.4` Transitive Reduction / Last-Occurrence DAG Sparsification in Maximum-Weight Closure).
- **Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal**:
  1. The problem statement is literally the textbook definition of **Maximum-Weight Closure**: $i \in C \text{ and } (j < i,\; a_j \mid a_i) \implies j \in C$.
  2. However, at $N = 3000$, adding an edge $i \xrightarrow{\infty} j$ for *every* $j < i$ with $a_j \mid a_i$ creates up to $\binom{3000}{2} \approx 4.5 \times 10^6$ edges!
  3. Look at the bound $a_i \in \{1, \dots, 100\}$: why is $A_{\max} = 100$ so tiny while $N = 3000$? Because **divisibility is transitive**! If $j_1 < j_2 < i$ and $a_{j_1} = a_{j_2}$ with $a_{j_2} \mid a_i$, then $j_2$ already has an $\infty$-arc $j_2 \xrightarrow{\infty} j_1$ (since $a_{j_1} \mid a_{j_2}$)!

::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic / Last-Occurrence Sparsification (#216)"}

Let $x_i \in \{0, 1\}$ ($x_i = 0 \iff i \in S$ chosen, $x_i = 1 \iff i \in T$ unchosen). For each index $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ and each distinct value $v \in \{1, \dots, 100\}$ that divides $a_i$, define:
$$\operatorname{last}(i, v) = \max\{\, j < i \mid a_j = v \,\}.$$

**Claim (Transitive Closure Equivalence)**: Wiring $i \xrightarrow{\infty} \operatorname{last}(i, v)$ for only the **most recent** occurrence $\operatorname{last}(i, v)$ of each divisor $v \mid a_i$ preserves the exact reachability closure of the full $O(N^2)$ graph!

*Proof*: Suppose $j < i$ satisfies $a_j = v \mid a_i$. Either $j = \operatorname{last}(i, v)$ (direct arc $i \xrightarrow{\infty} j$), or $j < j_1 = \operatorname{last}(i, v)$ with $a_{j_1} = v$. Since $v \mid v$, $j_1$ in turn connects to $j_2 = \operatorname{last}(j_1, v)$, forming a directed chain of $\infty$-arcs $i \xrightarrow{\infty} j_1 \xrightarrow{\infty} j_2 \xrightarrow{\infty} \dots \xrightarrow{\infty} j$! Thus $i \in S$ still forces $j \in S$, while the out-degree of vertex $i$ drops from $O(N)$ to at most $\max_{a \le 100} d(a) = 12$!

::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Codeforces 1473 F: Strange Set (#216)"}

#### Step 1–3: Mechanical Graph Compilation (`Ch 09.4`)

1. **Vertices & Terminal Arcs**: Create vertices $1 \dots N$, source $S = 0$, and sink $T = N + 1$. Initialize $\text{pos\_sum} = 0$ and array $\text{last}[1..100] \gets 0$.
2. **Single-Pass Sparsified DAG Construction ($i = 1 \dots N$)**:
   - If $b_i > 0$: add $\text{pos\_sum} \mathrel{+}= b_i$ and add $S \xrightarrow{b_i} i$.
   - If $b_i < 0$: add $i \xrightarrow{-b_i} T$.
   - For each divisor $v \in \{1, \dots, a_i\}$ with $v \mid a_i$:
     - If $\text{last}[v] > 0$, add directed arc $i \xrightarrow{\infty} \text{last}[v]$.
   - Update $\text{last}[a_i] \gets i$.
3. **Output**: Return $\text{pos\_sum} - \text{MaxFlow}(S, T)$. With $V = 3002$ and $E \le 3000 + 12 \times 3000 = 3.9 \times 10^4$, Dinic runs in $< 15\text{ ms}$.

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexamples (`FM-09`)

- **Toy Trace**: Let $N = 4$ with $a = [2, 2, 2, 6]$ and $b = [-5, 3, -2, 10]$.
  - $i = 1$ ($a_1 = 2, b_1 = -5$): $1 \xrightarrow{5} T$; $\text{last}[2] = 1$.
  - $i = 2$ ($a_2 = 2, b_2 = +3$): $S \xrightarrow{3} 2$, $2 \xrightarrow{\infty} 1$; $\text{last}[2] = 2$.
  - $i = 3$ ($a_3 = 2, b_3 = -2$): $3 \xrightarrow{2} T$, $3 \xrightarrow{\infty} 2$; $\text{last}[2] = 3$.
  - $i = 4$ ($a_4 = 6, b_4 = +10$): $S \xrightarrow{10} 4$, divisors of $6$ present in `last` is $v = 2 \implies 4 \xrightarrow{\infty} 3$.
  - Notice the chain $4 \xrightarrow{\infty} 3 \xrightarrow{\infty} 2 \xrightarrow{\infty} 1$: choosing $4 \in S$ forces $\{1, 2, 3, 4\} \subseteq S$ for net profit $10 - 2 + 3 - 5 = 6$.
- **Broken Gadget Counterexample (`FM-09` — Updating `last[a_i]` Only When $b_i < 0$, or Skipping $v = a_i$)**:
  - Suppose a coder thinks: *"Vertices with $b_j \ge 0$ are free profit anyway, so I only need to record $\text{last}[a_j] = j$ when $b_j < 0$!"*
  - Look at the toy trace above: $b_2 = +3 > 0$, while $b_1 = -5 < 0$. If you skip updating $\text{last}[2] = 2$ (or if you skip wiring $b_2 > 0$ to $\text{last}[2] = 1$), then choosing $2 \in S$ no longer forces $1 \in S$, falsely allowing $C = \{2\}$ with profit $+3$ without paying $b_1 = -5$! Every index $i$ must both link to $\text{last}[v]$ and update $\text{last}[a_i] \gets i$ regardless of the sign of $b_i$.

::::

### 3.2 Part III Failure Mode Self-Audit (`FM-09`–`FM-13`)

| Code | Failure Mode Name | Broken Habit / Symptom | Mathematical Root Cause | Mandatory Defensive Guard & Chapter Reference |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`FM-09`** | **Unpruned Closure Cycles, Reversed Prerequisite Arcs & Dense DAG Blowup** | Wiring prerequisite $u \xrightarrow{\infty} v$ instead of dependent $v \xrightarrow{\infty} u$ (`#209`); keeping mutually dependent cycles in sequential games (`Drill 1.1`); or adding $O(N^2)$ transitive closure arcs (`#216`). | In `Ch 09`, $x \in S \implies y \in S$ requires $x \xrightarrow{\infty} y$; simultaneous set closure includes positive-weight cycles that can never be unlocked sequentially; transitive edges are redundant. | Always translate *"choosing $v$ requires $u$"* as $v \xrightarrow{\infty} u$; run Kahn's indegree topological sort to delete cycle-locked nodes when sequential order is required; prune transitive arcs via `last[v]` ([Ch 09 §9.1–9.4](../chapters/ch09-maximum-weight-closure-project-selection.qmd)). |
| **`FM-10`** | **Inverted $T$-Side Clause Hubs & Unidirectional Grid Borders** | Wiring $B_j \xrightarrow{\infty} u$ on an All-$T$ subset bonus (`Drill 1.2`), or adding only $(r,c) \xrightarrow{1} (r,c+1)$ on an undirected partition cut (`#210`). | An arc pays its capacity only when tail $\in S$ and head $\in T$; $B_j \xrightarrow{\infty} u \to T$ has zero incoming capacity from $S$, so $B_j \in T$ cuts nothing! | All-$S$ bonus hub: $S \xrightarrow{W} B_A \xrightarrow{\infty} u$. All-$T$ bonus hub: $u \xrightarrow{\infty} B_B \xrightarrow{W} T$. Symmetric separation cost $c[x_u \neq x_v]$ requires **both** $u \xrightarrow{c} v$ and $v \xrightarrow{c} u$ ([Ch 10 §10.1–10.3](../chapters/ch10-pseudo-boolean-cuts-submodularity-burn-bury.qmd)). |
| **`FM-11`** | **Unflipped Supermodular Costs & Odd-Cycle Inversion Trap** | Trying to compile same-state penalty $w[x_u = x_v]$ or conflict $\infty \cdot x_u x_v$ without flipping one side (`#211`), or attempting bipartite inversion on a graph with triangles/odd cycles (`Drill 1.3`). | Direct $s$-$t$ cuts can only represent submodular tables ($B + C \ge A + D$). Variable inversion $y_v = 1 - x_v$ swaps $B+C \leftrightarrow A+D$ across cut edges $(u, v)$ iff the conflict graph is 2-colorable. | Verify 2-colorability ($G = L \sqcup R$) before substituting $y_v = 1 - x_v$ ($\forall v \in R$); orient hard conflict arcs strictly $L \xrightarrow{\infty} R$, never bidirectionally ([Ch 11 §11.1–11.3](../chapters/ch11-bipartite-variable-inversion-supermodular-rescue.qmd)). |
| **`FM-12`** | **Missing Reverse $\infty$-Monotonicity Locks on Unary Chains** | Omitting $(u, t+1) \xrightarrow{\infty} (u, t)$ on a $K$-state chain (`Drill 1.4`), or misaligning index offsets on $(u, t) \xrightarrow{\infty} (v, t - D)$. | Without reverse $\infty$-arcs, a cut can alternate $S \to T \to S \to T$ along column $u$'s chain, cutting two cheap edges to bypass an expensive middle state ($z_{u,t} = 0 < z_{u,t+1} = 1$). | Always add $(u, t+1) \xrightarrow{\infty} (u, t)$ for all $t = 1 \dots K-1$ so every unary chain satisfies $z_{u,1} \ge \dots \ge z_{u,K}$ and is cut forward exactly once ([Ch 12 §12.1–12.2](../chapters/ch12-multi-state-unary-chains-threshold-cuts.qmd)). |
| **`FM-13`** | **Non-Convex Ishikawa Penalties & Uncompressed Coordinate Chains** | Applying Ishikawa cross-differences to a concave/truncated function $\phi(d) = \min(|d|, \tau)$ (`Drill 1.5`), or building $O(N \cdot V_{\max})$ nodes when $V_{\max} = 10^9$ (`Drill 1.6`). | Ishikawa's cross-capacity $w = \frac{1}{2}\Delta^2 \phi(d)$ is non-negative iff $\phi$ is discrete convex ($\Delta^2 \phi \ge 0$). When $\phi(d) = |d|$ and $V_{\max} = 10^9$, Coarea level-set slicing decouples thresholds. | Check $\phi(d+1) - 2\phi(d) + \phi(d-1) \ge 0$ for all $d$ before using `Ch 13.1`; for $L_1$/convex data terms over huge ranges, slice by sorted target thresholds $b_{(k)}$ via Coarea (`Ch 13.2`) ([Ch 13 §13.1–13.3](../chapters/ch13-ishikawa-convex-penalties-coarea-parametric-cuts.qmd)). |

#### Five Rapid Self-Audit Verification Questions

Confirm that you can answer all five questions below from memory in under 60 seconds each:

1. **Question 1 (`FM-09`)**: In a project selection problem, choosing item $A$ requires choosing item $B$, and choosing item $B$ requires choosing item $C$. When $A \in S$ represents "chosen", what are the exact directions and capacities of the implication edges? Under what rule in the problem statement must you also run Kahn's indegree topological sort before Dinic?
2. **Question 2 (`FM-10`)**: You want to model a reward $+W$ granted if and only if $x_1 = x_2 = x_3 = 1$ (all three vertices placed on the $T$-side). Draw the auxiliary vertex $B$, its edge to $S$ or $T$, and the exact direction of the three $\infty$-edges between $B$ and $\{1, 2, 3\}$.
3. **Question 3 (`FM-11`)**: Given a $2 \times 2$ penalty table $c_{00} = 0, c_{01} = 0, c_{10} = 0, c_{11} = 10$ on an edge $(u, v)$, why does `Ch 10` compilation fail directly? After applying $y_v = 1 - x_v$ (`Ch 11`), what is the new $2 \times 2$ table in terms of $(x_u, y_v)$, and what single directed edge compiles it?
4. **Question 4 (`FM-12`)**: On a `切糕` unary chain where vertex $(u, k)$ represents the transition from height $k-1$ to $k$ ($k = 1 \dots R$, with $(u, 1) = S$-attached and $(u, R+1) = T$), why does the constraint $h_u - h_v \le D$ compile to $(u, k) \xrightarrow{\infty} (v, k - D)$, and what happens if $(v, k) \xrightarrow{\infty} (v, k-1)$ is omitted?
5. **Question 5 (`FM-13`)**: Why does $\phi(h_u - h_v) = (h_u - h_v)^2$ produce uniform cross-capacities $w_{(u, i) \to (v, j)} = 1$ for all $i, j$ in Ishikawa's construction, whereas $\phi(h_u - h_v) = |h_u - h_v|$ produces cross-capacities $w_{(u, i) \to (v, j)} = 1$ **only at the same level $i = j$** (decoupling into independent Coarea level-set cuts)?

## 4. Readiness Bridge to Part IV: Fractional Programming, Planar Duality, Min-Cut DP & Gomory–Hu Cut Trees

In **Part III (`Ch 09`–`Ch 13`)**, you mastered the **compilation half** of minimum-cut theory: translating non-graph algebraic objectives into a single static directed network $G = (V, E, c, s, t)$ and calling Dinic once. In **Part IV (`Ch 14`–`Ch 16`)**, we ask what happens when a single static Dinic call is no longer enough—either because the objective is a **nonlinear ratio** of two cut polynomials, or because $V$ and $E$ are **too large or queried too many times** for standard max-flow:

1. **From Static Project Selection (`Ch 09`) to Parametric Cuts & Maximum Density Subgraphs ([Ch 14](../chapters/ch14-fractional-programming-maximum-density-subgraphs.qmd))**:
   - In `#209` (*Gold Mine*) and `#216` (*Strange Set*), you maximized a linear sum $\sum_{i \in C} b_i - \sum_{e \in \text{cut}} c_e$.
   - In [Chapter 14](../chapters/ch14-fractional-programming-maximum-density-subgraphs.qmd), you will maximize **ratios** of closure quantities—such as Dinkelbach's 0-1 Fractional Programming $\max_C \frac{\sum_{i \in C} p_i}{\sum_{i \in C} w_i}$ and Goldberg's **Maximum Density Subgraph** $\max_{S \subseteq V} \frac{|E(S)|}{|S|}$—by embedding a `Ch 09` / `Ch 10` cut network inside a parametric binary search on $\lambda$ where node capacities vary continuously as $c_v(\lambda) = \lambda w_v - p_v$.
2. **From Grid Partition Cuts (`Ch 10`–`Ch 13`) to $(s, t)$-Planar Cycle–Cut Duality & Shortest Paths ([Ch 15](../chapters/ch15-planar-cycle-cut-duality-shortest-paths.qmd))**:
   - In `#210` (*Wolves and Sheep*) and `#214` (*Cross*), you ran Dinic on $100 \times 100$ grids ($V = 10^4$). What if the grid is $1000 \times 1000$ ($V = 10^6$), where Dinic times out?
   - In [Chapter 15](../chapters/ch15-planar-cycle-cut-duality-shortest-paths.qmd), when the cut network is **$(s, t)$-planar** (or general planar), every minimum $s$-$t$ cut bijects with a **shortest path in the planar dual graph $G^*$**, replacing $O(V^{1.5})$ Dinic with $O(V \log V)$ Dijkstra (`[ICPC-Beijing 2006] 狼抓兔子` and `[NOI2010] 海拔`).
3. **From Explicit Cut Graphs (`Ch 09`–`Ch 13`) to Min-Cut DP, Stoer–Wagner & Gomory–Hu Cut Trees ([Ch 16](../chapters/ch16-mincut-dp-global-mincut-gomory-hu-trees.qmd))**:
   - Whenever a `Ch 10`–`Ch 13` cut graph has bounded treewidth, small corridor width, or complete-bipartite cardinality symmetry (like `ARC 125 E Snack` or `CF 724 E Goods Transportation`), [Chapter 16](../chapters/ch16-mincut-dp-global-mincut-gomory-hu-trees.qmd) shows how to **eliminate the flow solver altogether** and compute $\text{MinCut}(S, T)$ directly via **Dynamic Programming over the $S/T$ partition**. Finally, for undirected graphs queried across all $\binom{N}{2}$ terminal pairs, Gusfield's **Gomory–Hu Cut Tree** compresses all $\binom{N}{2}$ minimum cuts into $N - 1$ Dinic calls.

### 4.1 Part III Algebraic-to-Graph Compilation Cheat Sheet

Keep this master compilation table beside you as you enter Parts IV–VI:

| Pseudo-Boolean / Multi-State Clause ($x_u = [u \in T] \in \{0,1\}$) | Submodularity / Structural Condition | Mechanical $s$-$t$ Cut Gadget |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Maximize $\sum_{u} w_u (1 - x_u)$ s.t. $u \in S \implies v \in S$** (`Ch 09`, `#209`, `#216`) | Any directed graph (prune cycles if sequential order required) | $\text{Base} = \sum_{w_u > 0} w_u$; $S \xrightarrow{w_u} u$ ($w_u > 0$), $u \xrightarrow{-w_u} T$ ($w_u < 0$), $u \xrightarrow{\infty} v$ |
| **Pairwise asymmetric penalty $c_{01}(1 - x_u)x_v + c_{10}x_u(1 - x_v)$** (`Ch 10`, `#210`, `#214`) | Submodular: $c_{01} + c_{10} \ge c_{00} + c_{11}$ | Add directed arc $u \xrightarrow{c_{01}} v$ and reverse arc $v \xrightarrow{c_{10}} u$ |
| **Edge-compressed pairwise bonus $E_A(1-x_u)(1-x_v) + E_B x_u x_v$** (`Ch 10.4`) | Always submodular ($E_A, E_B \ge 0$) | Add $\frac{1}{2}E_A$ to $S \to u, S \to v$; add $\frac{1}{2}E_B$ to $u \to T, v \to T$; add $u \xleftrightarrow{\frac{1}{2}(E_A+E_B)} v$ |
| **All-$S$ subset bonus $+W \prod_{u \in A} (1 - x_u)$** (`Ch 10.3`) | $W \ge 0$, arbitrary subset $A \subseteq V$ | Add $+W$ to base; create hub $B_A$ with $S \xrightarrow{W} B_A$ and $B_A \xrightarrow{\infty} u$ ($\forall u \in A$) |
| **All-$T$ subset bonus $+W \prod_{u \in A} x_u$** (`Ch 10.3`, `Drill 1.2`) | $W \ge 0$, arbitrary subset $A \subseteq V$ | Add $+W$ to base; create hub $B_B$ with $u \xrightarrow{\infty} B_B$ ($\forall u \in A$) and $B_B \xrightarrow{W} T$ |
| **Supermodular conflict $\infty \cdot x_u x_v$ or same-state penalty $w[x_u = x_v]$** (`Ch 11`, `#211`) | Conflict graph $G = (L \sqcup R, E)$ **must be bipartite** | Invert $R$: $y_u = 1 - x_u$ ($u \in L$), $y_v = x_v$ ($v \in R$); wire $L \xrightarrow{\infty} R$ (or $L \xleftrightarrow{w} R$) |
| **Destroy all 4-vertex patterns across a 4-colorable grid** (`Ch 11`+`Ch 12`, `#212`) | Every forbidden pattern maps to $C_1 \to C_2 \to C_3 \to C_4$ | Split $i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{w_i} i_{\text{out}}$ and wire $S \xrightarrow{\infty} C_1 \xrightarrow{\infty} C_2 \xrightarrow{\infty} C_3 \xrightarrow{\infty} C_4 \xrightarrow{\infty} T$ |
| **Multi-state choice $h_u \in \{1..K\}$ with $h_u - h_v \le D$** (`Ch 12`, `Drill 1.4`) | Arbitrary $w(u, k) \ge 0$, integer offset $D \in \mathbb{Z}$ | Chain $(u, 1) \xrightarrow{w(u,1)} \dots \xrightarrow{w(u,K)} T$, reverse $(u, k+1) \xrightarrow{\infty} (u, k)$, diagonal $(u, k) \xrightarrow{\infty} (v, k-D)$ |
| **Convex difference penalty $\phi(h_u - h_v)$** (`Ch 13.1`, `Drill 1.5`) | Discrete convex: $\Delta^2 \phi(d) = \phi(d+1) - 2\phi(d) + \phi(d-1) \ge 0$ | Unary chains with cross-arcs $(u, i) \to (v, j)$ of capacity $\frac{1}{2}\Delta^2 \phi(i - j)$ |
| **Large-range $L_1$ Coarea $\sum c_u |h_u - b_u| + \sum w_{uv}|h_u - h_v|$** (`Ch 13.2`, `Drill 1.6`) | $b_u \in [0, 10^9]$, $c_u, w_{uv} \ge 0$ | Slice by sorted targets $b_{(1)} < \dots < b_{(K)}$; solve decoupled binary cuts $z_u(t) = [h_u > t]$ |
